title: The Gender Pain Gap - Gender-specific differences in prehospital pain therapy. Truth or myth?
summary:
The gender pain gap is a term used in public health research to describe the differences in the care provided to men and women with chronic pain. The differences in the care provided to these patients are not limited to Germany but are evident in varying degrees throughout Europe. Whether the differences shown in this study are also evident in the treatment of acute pain in emergency situations is by no means certain and is the subject of the planned investigation. Whether the term gender pain gap can be used appropriately in this context or whether it represents an inadmissible transfer of the care situation for chronic pain to pain therapy in emergency situations also depends on the results of the planned investigation. 
The aim of the study is to systematically record and analyze any gender-specific differences in preclinical pain management for various disease and injury patterns by emergency physicians. The study will examine whether patients receive different levels of care in terms of the implementation and intensity of pain management in emergency situations. Based on the results, possible inequalities in treatment will be identified, their possible causes examined, and concrete recommendations for gender-equitable and evidence-based pain management in emergency medicine will be derived. In the long term, the study aims to contribute to improving the quality of care and promoting non-discriminatory emergency medical practice.

interventions.name: Primary and secondary operations of the ground and helicopter emergency service.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Primary and secondary operations of the ground and helicopter emergency service
Exclusion criteria:
Patients with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score < 11 at any point in time.
All patients with airway management
